title: Vote to approve the Wilsonville Town Center Development District
ballot_label: Caption: Vote to approve the Wilsonville Town Center Development District. Question: Should the City adopt proposed Ordinance No. 905 establishing the Wilsonville Town Center Development District, an urban renewal district?
summary: Asks Wilsonville voters whether to adopt Ordinance No. 905 creating the Town Center Development District, an urban renewal district using tax increment financing to fund gathering spaces and parking, small-business incentives and infrastructure in Town Center. The plan sets maximum indebtedness of $152 million ($85.5 million in today's dollars) over a 28-year duration. The ballot summary states TIF is not a new tax or tax rate increase.
yes_means: A yes vote approves adoption of Ordinance No. 905, establishing the Wilsonville Town Center Development District as an urban renewal district.
no_means: A no vote rejects Ordinance No. 905, and the Town Center Development District urban renewal district would not be formed.
fiscal_impact: Per the ballot title and city ordinance page: maximum indebtedness (spending cap) of $152 million ($85.5 M in today's dollars), structured as smaller borrowings, 28-year duration with tax increment collection anticipated through fiscal year 2056; the measure would not establish a new property tax or increase existing tax rates.

arguments.author: Mark Smith, Wilsonville (letter to the editor)
arguments.statement: In a September 2026 letter to the Wilsonville Spokesman, Mark Smith urges a yes vote on Measure 3-641 for community gathering spaces, local employment and food carts.
arguments.excerpt: There are many reasons to vote YES on Measure 3-641 to approve the Wilsonville Town Center Development District.

arguments.author: Mark Smith, Wilsonville (letter to the editor)
arguments.statement: Mark Smith writes that urban renewal would fund infrastructure rather than come from residents' property taxes, responding to claims it hurts the city budget.
arguments.excerpt: urban renewal will fund infrastructure, not our property taxes

arguments.author: Eric Winters, Wilsonville resident (opinion column)
arguments.statement: In an October 2026 Wilsonville Spokesman opinion column, Eric Winters says the city's feasibility study projects 96.4% of new housing would be apartments, mostly market-rate.
arguments.excerpt: By the city’s own feasibility study, 96.4% will be apartments. Not affordable housing for Wilsonville’s low-income families, but premium market-rate apartments for thousands of new residents.

arguments.author: Eric Winters, Wilsonville resident (opinion column)
arguments.statement: Winters says new residents would add traffic to Wilsonville Road and the I-5 interchange, which he describes as already congested with no funded state fix.
arguments.excerpt: Thousands of new residents and their cars would funnel onto Wilsonville Road and the I-5 interchange, already the most congested corridor in the city, with no state fix funded and no timeline.

arguments.author: Eric Winters, Wilsonville resident (opinion column)
arguments.statement: Winters notes the plan could involve up to $152 million repaid by diverting property tax growth through 2056.
arguments.excerpt: Up to $152 million, repaid by diverting property tax growth through 2056.

arguments.author: Doris Wehler, Wilsonville (letter to the editor)
arguments.statement: In a September 2026 letter, Doris Wehler says the project would require 2,381 housing units to finance it and that taxpayers do not need to underwrite the plan.
arguments.excerpt: What the city doesn't advertise is the 2,381 housing units that will be required to finance this urban renewal project.

gaps: Official county voters' pamphlet explanatory statement and any filed YES/NO arguments could not be read (pamphlet text extraction truncated before the measure pages, in both the Clackamas and Washington County pamphlets).
No YES argument from a named campaign committee or city official on the merits found in T1/T3 sources; YES side is represented only by one letter to the editor.
collection_notes: yes_means/no_means: Oregon local ballot titles carry no official result-of-vote statement; these are neutral one-sentence descriptions written by the collector strictly from the official ballot question/summary. County voters' pamphlet (https://docs.clackamas.us/documents/drupal/03f4f9db-a1ab-4a1f-9ce1-16059d49a513) lists this measure in its index, but WebFetch text extraction ends at page C-33 (~117k chars), before the measure section, so the pamphlet's explanatory statement and any filed arguments could not be read. The county ballot-title PDF linked from the election page returned only the multilingual accommodations notice (likely an image scan). Ballot title text taken from the City's Notice of Receipt of Ballot Title (filed Aug 6, 2026). Washington County pamphlet (https://www.washingtoncountyor.gov/elections/documents/november-3-2026-voters-pamphlet/download?inline) lists 3-641 at WC-47-50 but extraction also truncated at WC-29. Many 2026 Wilsonville Spokesman pieces (April-May) concern the earlier May 2026 urban renewal measure (3-632) and were not used. Wilsonville Spokesman (wilsonvillespokesman.com) is the local bylined newspaper (formerly Pamplin); classified T3. Letters to the editor are used as attributed opinion only; YES side has fewer items because only one supportive letter was found with equal search effort (YES-specific search also run). Aug 7 Spokesman article quotes about the referral process (Dempsey, Cunningham, O'Neil) were not used as they concern ballot-title process, not the measure's merits. Inventory title matches the county caption (no trailing period).
